prompt: A packet crosses an interface and matches none of the ACL's lines. What happens to it?
hint: Look at the last row but one of the table.

choices.text: It passes, since no line refused it
choices.why: An ACL ends in a deny you cannot see.

choices.text: It is forwarded and counted as unmatched
choices.why: Unmatched packets are not forwarded.

choices.text: The implicit deny drops it
choices.why: Right. It sits at the end, invisible in the configuration.

choices.text: It goes to the ACL on the other direction
choices.why: Each direction's list decides alone.

prompt: An ACL has line 10 `permit tcp any any eq 80` and line 20 `deny ip host 10.0.0.5 any`. 10.0.0.5 sends a packet to port 80. What happens?
hint: Lines are compared from the top.

choices.text: Denied, because a deny line outranks a permit line
choices.why: There is no ranking by action; order decides.

choices.text: Denied, because the line naming the host is more specific
choices.why: That is how a routing table chooses, not an ACL.

choices.text: Permitted, and logged as a conflict between lines
choices.why: Nothing detects a conflict; line 20 is simply never reached.

choices.text: Permitted by line 10
choices.why: Right. The first line that matches decides.

prompt: Match each property to how an ACL has it.

pairs.right: none: each packet is judged alone

prompt: What does a standard ACL test in a packet?
hint: It says who, and not where.

choices.text: Its source and destination addresses
choices.why: The destination is an extended ACL's field.

choices.text: Its source address
choices.why: Right. Nothing else.

choices.text: Its source address and its port
choices.why: Ports need an extended ACL.

choices.text: The destination it is heading for
choices.why: It is the opposite field.

prompt: With the standard ACL loaded on branch, what did guest's probe report for remote:80 and remote:443?

choices.text: 80 open and 443 blocked
choices.why: A standard ACL cannot tell ports apart.

choices.text: Both refused, answered by the router
choices.why: Nothing answered; the packets were dropped.

choices.text: Both open, because guest shares branchpc's segment
choices.why: The ACL tests the address, not the segment.

choices.text: Both blocked
choices.why: Right. Every destination and port, since only the source is tested.

prompt: Why does the nftables version carry a line accepting ARP that the IOS ACL does not need?
hint: How early does the netdev hook see traffic?

choices.text: The ingress hook sees every frame, and dropping ARP would stop the machines finding the router
choices.why: Right. A router's IP ACL never sees ARP.

choices.text: ARP carries the source address the ACL tests
choices.why: The line accepts ARP whatever it carries.

choices.text: nft refuses a chain whose rules are all IP
choices.why: The chain would load; the segment would break.

choices.text: It replaces the implicit deny
choices.why: policy drop is the implicit deny.

prompt: Before any ACL, remote:22 was refused. With the extended ACL, it is blocked. What does that change show?

choices.text: remote stopped its SSH server
choices.why: It had none; that is why it refused.

choices.text: The SYN no longer reaches remote
choices.why: Right. Refused was remote's reset; blocked is silence.

choices.text: The router now answers with a reset on remote's behalf
choices.why: A reset would still read as refused.

choices.text: remote's firewall started to drop port 22
choices.why: The counter on branch caught it.

prompt: How many packets had the web line (tcp dport 80, 443) counted after the test?
Which of these can an extended ACL test that a standard ACL does not? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The destination address
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The source address
choices.why: Both kinds test it; it is the standard ACL's one field.

choices.text: The protocol, such as tcp or udp
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whether the packet belongs to a connection already open
choices.why: An ACL keeps no state, of either kind.

choices.text: The TCP or UDP port
choices.why: Right.

prompt: What is the third byte of the wildcard mask for a /20?

Which wildcard mask matches the network 10.8.4.0/22?

prompt: Which addresses does `192.168.0.1 0.0.254.0` match?
hint: Write 254 in binary: which bit must match?

choices.text: Every address from 192.168.0.1 to 192.168.254.1
choices.why: The lowest bit of the third byte must be 0, so odd values are out.
Every 1 bit in 254 is free, so many values match.

choices.text: The whole of 192.168.0.0/16
choices.why: The last byte must be 1.

choices.text: Host .1 in every even third byte

prompt: Where does a standard ACL belong, and why?

choices.text: Close to the source, so unwanted traffic is dropped as early as possible
choices.why: That is the rule for an extended ACL.

choices.text: Close to the destination, since it knows the source and nothing more
choices.why: Right. Near the source it would cut that source off from everything.

choices.text: On the router's internet side, outbound
choices.why: The kind of ACL decides the place, not the internet.

choices.text: Anywhere, since it tests a single field
choices.why: That single field is exactly why the place matters.

prompt: Why is an inbound ACL usually preferred over an outbound one?

choices.text: Outbound ACLs cannot test source addresses
choices.why: Both directions test the same fields.

choices.text: Inbound ACLs keep connection state
choices.why: Neither direction keeps state.

choices.text: It drops before routing, and it protects the router
choices.why: Right. Outbound cannot protect the router itself.

choices.text: Outbound ACLs run in software and inbound in hardware
choices.why: The section does not split them that way.

prompt: Which packets does the IOS `established` keyword match?
hint: It reads a flag, not a table.

choices.text: Packets of connections the router saw open
choices.why: An ACL keeps no table of connections.

choices.text: A connection's first SYN
choices.why: That is what it fails.

choices.text: Any reply, TCP or UDP
choices.why: It exists for TCP alone.

choices.text: TCP packets with ACK or RST set
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A TCP packet with ACK set, belonging to no connection, reaches a line with `established`. What happens?
hint: The line checks a flag the sender sets.

choices.text: It passes, and the host answers with a reset
choices.why: Right. No connection opens, but the ACL let it through.

choices.text: The line drops it, as no connection exists
choices.why: The line has no idea whether one exists.

choices.text: It passes and the host opens a connection
choices.why: The host resets it; nothing is open.

choices.text: The router answers it with a reset
choices.why: The ACL passes or drops; the host answers.

prompt: An inbound ACL uses `established` for web replies. How do the branch's DNS answers get in?

choices.text: Through the same line, since a DNS answer has ACK set
choices.why: UDP has no ACK flag.

choices.text: Through a line of their own permitting source port 53
choices.why: Right. And that line is lesson 1's hole.

choices.text: They cannot; the implicit deny drops them
choices.why: A line for them can be written.

choices.text: Through an `established` on a udp line
choices.why: The keyword is for TCP.

prompt: With the extended ACL on branch, the branch's machines stop syncing time over NTP (UDP 123), and the implicit-deny counter rises. Why?

choices.text: established blocks UDP replies
choices.why: The NTP request never left the LAN.

choices.text: The wildcard 0.0.0.255 on the permit lines leaves the NTP servers out
choices.why: The destination is any; the wildcard is on the source.

choices.text: No line permits udp 123, so the implicit deny takes it
choices.why: Right. The counter is where it shows.

choices.text: The arp line catches NTP before the UDP line
choices.why: NTP is IP, not ARP.

prompt: A standard ACL reads `access-list 20 permit 172.16.8.0 0.0.7.255`. Which source does it permit?
hint: The third byte may be 8 plus anything up to 7.

choices.why: 16 is past 8 + 7.
7 is below the network's 8.
24 is outside 8 to 15.
Right. 8 to 15 in the third byte.
